reason: The Cordero radii of As (119 pm) and Se (120 pm) differ by 1 pm, inside the dataset's own uncertainty: by group 15-16 of period 4 the across-period contraction has flattened because the filled 3d shell shields the added nuclear charge poorly.
As (119 pm) and Br (120 pm) are 1 pm apart, within the Cordero uncertainty: the period-4 p-block radii level off after the 3d shell fills, so the across-period shrink is essentially gone by bromine.

Te (138 pm) and I (139 pm) differ by 1 pm, inside the dataset's uncertainty: the across-period contraction has flattened by the end of period 5 as the 4d shell shields poorly and the bonds measured are to larger partners.
Tl (145 pm) and Pb (146 pm) are 1 pm apart: in the period-6 p-block the across-period shrink is cancelled by the inert-pair 6s contraction and poor 4f/5d shielding, leaving the radii nearly flat.

Period-6 p-block radii are nearly flat (Tl 145, Pb 146, Bi 148 pm) because relativistic 6s contraction and poor 4f/5d shielding offset the usual across-period decrease, and Bi's three 6p electrons sit in the slightly larger 6p3/2 level.

Astatine's Cordero radius (150 pm) is an estimate from very few structures, and the period-6 p-block radii are nearly flat anyway, so the across-period shrink from Tl (145 pm) does not show in this dataset.
Pb (146 pm) and Bi (148 pm) are 2 pm apart in a period whose p-block radii barely change: the inert-pair 6s contraction and poor 4f/5d shielding cancel the usual across-period decrease.

Astatine's Cordero radius (150 pm) rests on very few structures and comes out larger than lead's (146 pm); the period-6 p-block radii are nearly flat, so a small data artifact is enough to flip the order.
Astatine's 150 pm Cordero value is an estimate from scarce structural data and exceeds bismuth's 148 pm; across the flat period-6 p-block that 2 pm difference is within the method's uncertainty.
Polonium's Cordero radius (140 pm) comes from few structures and astatine's (150 pm) from fewer still; the 10 pm jump is a data artifact of a sparsely measured corner of the table, not a trend.
Boron's outermost electron is in 2p, higher in energy and better shielded than beryllium's paired 2s electrons, so it is easier to remove despite the extra proton.
Oxygen's fourth 2p electron must pair up in an already occupied orbital, and that pairing repulsion makes it easier to remove than one of nitrogen's three unpaired, half-filled 2p electrons.
Aluminum's outermost electron is in 3p, higher in energy and better shielded than magnesium's paired 3s electrons, so it is easier to remove despite the extra proton.
Aluminum's single 3p electron is unusually easy to remove (the s-to-p drop), while calcium is removing one of a filled 4s pair, so the heavier element edges ahead.
Gallium's 4p electron sits outside a filled 3d shell that shields the nucleus poorly, so the extra nuclear charge pulls it slightly harder than expected and the usual drop down the group vanishes.
Thallium's 6p electron is held by a nucleus poorly shielded by the 4f and 5d shells, with relativistic contraction adding to the pull, so its ionization energy is higher than aluminum's.
Sulfur's fourth 3p electron must pair up, and the pairing repulsion makes it easier to remove than one of phosphorus's three unpaired, half-filled 3p electrons.
Gallium's single 4p electron is higher in energy than calcium's paired 4s electrons, so even with eleven more protons gallium's first ionization energy comes out lower.
Thallium's 6p electron feels a nucleus poorly shielded by the 4f and 5d shells, and relativistic effects contract the inner shells further, so it is held more tightly than gallium's 4p electron.
Selenium's fourth 4p electron must pair up, and the pairing repulsion makes it slightly easier to remove than one of arsenic's three unpaired 4p electrons.
The 4f and 5d shells shield thallium's 6p electron poorly (the lanthanide contraction), so the nucleus holds it tighter than indium holds its 5p electron.
Lead's 6p electrons are held by a nucleus poorly shielded by the 4f and 5d shells, with relativistic contraction adding to the pull, so lead's ionization energy edges above tin's.
In period 6 the 6p level splits strongly by spin-orbit coupling; bismuth's third 6p electron goes into the higher 6p3/2 level and is easier to remove than one of lead's lower 6p1/2 pair.
Gallium's 4p electrons sit outside a filled 3d shell that shields the nucleus poorly, so gallium pulls bonding electrons harder than aluminum (the d-block contraction).
Indium's valence electrons sit outside a filled 4d shell that shields poorly, so its electronegativity stays above aluminum's instead of falling down the group.
Thallium's valence electrons are held by a nucleus poorly shielded by the 4f and 5d shells, with relativistic contraction adding to the pull, so it is more electronegative than aluminum.
Germanium's 4p electrons sit outside a filled 3d shell that shields the nucleus poorly, so germanium pulls bonding electrons slightly harder than silicon (the d-block contraction).
Tin's valence electrons sit outside filled 3d and 4d shells that shield poorly, so its electronegativity stays just above silicon's instead of falling down the group.
The 4f and 5d shells shield thallium's valence electrons poorly and relativistic contraction tightens its hold, so thallium is slightly more electronegative than indium.
Xenon's Pauling value (2.6) is derived from its few compounds with fluorine and oxygen, and a noble gas does not continue the across-period rise, so iodine comes out higher.
Argon's dominant isotope is Ar-40 while potassium's is K-39, so argon averages heavier even with one fewer proton; Earth's Ar-40 is abundant because it is the decay product of K-40.
Tellurium's most abundant isotopes are the heavy Te-128 and Te-130, while iodine is a single isotope, I-127, so tellurium's average mass exceeds iodine's despite the lower atomic number.
